extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, taxonomists, philosophers of science, and students of scientific method and classification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing scientific classifications and nomenclatures: how to form natural groups (species, genera, families), choose characters or types, handle anomalies, and arrange groups into series suited to inductive inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-sensitive classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification depends on the purpose for which objects are considered; different arts or sciences classify according to properties relevant to their practical ends (e.g., a farmer divides plants into useful plants and weeds; a botanist into dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the properties to classify by according to the practical or intellectual end you pursue. A legal or practical context may justify a different classification than one aimed at extending general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural group criterion (choose attributes that most mark individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying objects to extend knowledge of their whole properties and relations, consider as most important those attributes which contribute most to render the things like one another and unlike other things; these give the class the most marked individuality and may be called natural groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize attributes that occupy the largest role in the object's existence and would most impress an unbiased observer; these should form the basis of natural classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as determining marks of groups (Mill's critique of Type-only doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural groups are determined by characters (definite marks), not solely by reference to a Type; the problem is to find a few definite characters which point to the multitude of indefinite ones and mark which side of a kind-barrier an object belongs to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely only on resemblance to a type-specimen. Enumerate characters that serve as reliable indicators of common parentage or membership; the enumeration of characters is the definition of the species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Type as illustrative exemplar, not sole determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: A Type is an example of a class considered as eminently possessing the character of the class; species nearer the type are arranged about it, deviating in degree and direction; however, the class is not determined solely by resemblance to the type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a type-species or type-genus as a mental standard to illustrate and help recognize class-membership, especially where indefinite characters are numerous, but verify membership by characters, not by mere resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for anomalies and imperfect diagnoses
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of natural groups may include statements of what usually happens rather than absolute rules; anomalies occur commonly (e.g., some Rosaceæ genera lack stipules or possess albumen), so an artificial diagnosis may be imperfect and yield to general weight of affinities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit exceptions when an object agrees with most of the class's characters; include anomalous specimens if overall affinity is greater than affinity to other groups. Treat anomalous features as expected and document them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that classes admit general assertions (characters must enable predication)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a class did not possess any characters in common, no general assertions would be possible; every natural class should possess characters making general assertions possible as knowledge grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure chosen characters are sufficient to support general statements or predictions about class-members' properties, i.e., the class should be definable by characters that allow induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of few decisive characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a few definite characters which point to the multitude of indefinite properties — marks whereby we may determine on which side of the barrier an object takes its place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer characters that reliably indicate membership and correlate with many other (possibly unknown) properties; when possible choose characters that are themselves important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and priority of distinctions of Kind
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist distinctions of Kind that run through the whole nature of things; where distinctions of Kind exist, classification should recognize and adopt them, because these lead to classes whose members share innumerable properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where evidence indicates a true distinction of Kind (e.g., major anatomical or physiological divides), let classification reflect that as foundational rather than relying on superficial or arbitrary distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of classes: infimæ species then aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: After recognizing and defining the lowest real kinds (infimæ species), arrange those into larger groups, making these correspond to Kinds wherever possible, otherwise grouping by resemblance and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build classification from well-defined lowest units upward; where higher groups are not genuine Kinds, ensure they are formed out of species sharing important characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature should convey maximal information and economize memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific names of Kinds are defined by the characters of the class; their merit beyond this is to convey as much information as possible by name-formation so that a person knowing the term gets assistance remembering the thing and someone ignorant gains knowledge from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible make names indicate key properties (ideal in chemistry); otherwise construct names to indicate proximate natural affinities (binary nomenclature) to maximize mnemonic and informational value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary (and where needed ternary) nomenclature principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary nomenclature — composing species names of the genus name plus a specific epithet — indicates the proximate natural group and economizes names; where binary is insufficient a ternary construction (species, genus, order) may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genus+specific epithet as standard (botany/zoology); accept historical or conventional specific names when necessary. Consider ternary systems in domains where more hierarchical signalling is needed (example: mineralogical proposals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by series for facilitating particular inductive inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: When classification is intended to facilitate the study of a particular phenomenon, bring into one class all Kinds that exhibit that phenomenon and arrange them in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it, from those which exhibit most to those which exhibit least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To study a law via concomitant variations, order instances by degree of the phenomenon; this ordering aids detection of causes or common causal relations and is indispensable when applying the Method of Concomitant Variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-species indispensable for series (identify highest degree exemplar)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a series based on degrees of a phenomenon, assume a type-species that exhibits the properties constitutive of the class in the highest degree; other varieties are considered as degeneracies from that type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the exemplar in which the phenomenon is most developed to reveal subsidiary phenomena and to make recognition of lesser degrees possible; study highest-degree instances for fuller effects and collateral circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary divisions grounded on variations in the main phenomenon's degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary divisions (orders, families) must be grounded not on all distinctions indiscriminately but on those which correspond to variations in the degree of the main phenomenon; break the series where variations begin to be attended by conspicuous changes in miscellaneous properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subdividing, prefer distinctions that reflect real steps in intensity or character of the principal phenomenon (e.g., Sensation, Thought, Voluntary Motion in animals) so that groups correspond to definite portions of the scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of natural affinity to the principle of the series
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural affinity remains the main principle of division, but these principles must be applied in subordination to the needs of a natural series; groups must not be constituted so as to place together things that should occupy different points on the general scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure families and genera, where practicable, represent contiguous positions on the general scale; only when impossible may subdivisions be based on characters not connected with the main phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits of series-classification across domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification by natural series has been practicable chiefly in animals (where a dominant phenomenon—animal life—orders differences); in plants the series is harder to establish beyond natural groups because gradations in vegetative phenomena do not yield a univocal scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize domain limitations: attempt series-classification principally where a dominant phenomenon pervades and orders other properties; avoid forcing series where it is not natural or informative.
